newsitem.title: USA: New Hampshire court strikes repressed memories.
newsitem.headline: New Hampshire court strikes repressed memories.

text.p: The New Hampshire Supreme Court on Tuesday said so-called recovered memories of past sexual abuse and other traumas were not automatically admissible as evidence.
"We do not mean to suggest that ... recovered repressed memories are 'false.' We merely recognise that the memories are subject to many factors that may affect their reliability," the court wrote.

State prosecutors requested the ruling after a superior court judge refused to allow alleged rape victims to testify in two different sexual assault cases. Both victims claimed that they remembered being raped after undergoing therapy for depression.

In the case of a Manchester woman who claimed her seventh grade teacher had sexually assaulted her, more than five years had passed between the time of the alleged incident and when the memories were "recovered" during a therapy session.
The other sexual assault case involved an Amherst woman in her 20s who had claimed that her father had assaulted her when she was a teenager.

In both instances the women remembered the alleged assaults after undergoing therapy. The state sought prosecution using evidence obtained from so-called Repressed Memory Syndrome. A lower court had ruled in both cases that memories brought to light during therapy do not pass rules of evidence under New Hampshire law.
The Supreme Court said there was not yet enough scientific understanding of repressed memory syndrome to allow it as evidence.
